concepts.name: The state and the government
concepts.description: The four features of a state, what a government is and why the words are confused.
concepts.idea: The state has people, land, government and sovereignty; the government is only one part and can change.
concepts.rule: A state (or nation) is a political organisation with authority to govern a defined territory and its population. It has four parts: people, land, government and sovereignty, the full power to make laws and decisions without outside control. Without a permanent population there is no state; tourists who visit do not form one. Boundaries are agreed with neighbouring states. The government is a group of people or system that runs the country: leaders, ministers and officials who make, enforce laws and resolve disputes. It can change after elections but the state remains, like teachers coming and going while the school stays. The words are mixed up because the government acts on behalf of the state and we mostly meet the government.
concepts.example: The state is like a school and the government is the principal and teachers.

questions.q: After a general election the ruling party is defeated and a new ministry takes office, with new ministers and a changed policy direction. Of the four parts of a state described in the Class 7 chapter, the one that has changed is
questions.a: the government, while the people, the land and the sovereignty remain as before
o: the government, while the people, the land and the sovereignty remain as before
the sovereignty, because the new ministry now takes the decisions that were taken by the earlier one
the people, because the electorate has chosen differently and the earlier citizens' group no longer rules
the state itself, because the authority of the earlier government to govern the territory has ended
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.146: the government is just one part of the state; it can change after elections but the state remains the same, like teachers who come and go while the school remains.
w: Rejected: sovereignty is the state's full power to make laws without outside control and does not pass from one ministry to the next (p.144, 145).
Rejected: the people form the permanent population, which does not change because the ministry does (p.145).
Rejected: the state continues; only the government changes after elections (p.146).

questions.q: A country has a clearly marked territory, a settled population and an elected ministry, but its laws can be set aside by a foreign power. Judged by the four parts of a state in the Class 7 chapter, the element that is missing is
questions.a: sovereignty, the full power to make laws and take decisions without outside control
o: sovereignty, the full power to make laws and take decisions without outside control
a permanent population, because the people do not identify with the territory they live in
a government, because a ministry whose laws can be set aside is not a system to run the country
a defined territory, because its boundaries have not been agreed upon with the neighbouring states
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.144-145: sovereignty means complete control over its own matters and no outside interference in internal affairs; the scenario gives people, land and a ministry but denies this.
w: Rejected: the scenario states that the population is settled (p.145).
Rejected: the scenario states that an elected ministry exists and runs the country; the fault lies in sovereignty (p.146).
Rejected: the scenario states that the territory is clearly marked (p.145).

questions.q: A note in the Class 7 chapter points out that in India the word 'State' is used in two senses. In the expressions 'the State of Kerala' and 'the Indian State', the word refers respectively to
questions.a: a subnational unit of the country, and the sovereign political organisation of the whole country
o: a subnational unit of the country, and the sovereign political organisation of the whole country
the government of Kerala headed by its Chief Minister, and the Union Government alone
a district-level unit of administration, and the Union Government together with Parliament
the legislature of Kerala, and the Parliament of India, both being law-making bodies
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.146 ('Don't Miss Out'): 'state' can refer to the Indian State or to subnational units like Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu or Kerala (the State of Kerala). The Indian State is the political organisation with the four parts of a state described on p.144.
w: Rejected: the chapter treats the State as more than any one government (p.146).
Rejected: Kerala is a subnational unit of the country, not a district (p.146).
Rejected: the legislature is one organ of government, not the meaning given to 'State' (p.146, 148).

questions.q: In 1949 India declared the continuation of her full membership of the Commonwealth of Nations, accepting the British Crown as its head, and India is also a member of the United Nations. According to Laxmikanth, the bearing of these two facts on India's sovereignty is that
questions.a: neither the Commonwealth declaration nor the membership of the United Nations limits India's sovereignty in any manner
o: neither the Commonwealth declaration nor the membership of the United Nations limits India's sovereignty in any manner
the Commonwealth declaration makes India a dominion in external matters, while the United Nations membership leaves sovereignty untouched
United Nations membership restricts India's freedom in external affairs, although the Commonwealth declaration does not affect sovereignty
both place limits on India's external sovereignty, though her sovereignty in internal affairs remains complete
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble, p.86: the 1949 declaration is extra-constitutional and does not affect India's sovereignty in any manner, and UN membership too is in no way a limitation on her sovereignty. India is neither a dependency nor a dominion of any nation.
w: Rejected: the book says India is not a dominion of any other nation and the declaration does not affect sovereignty (p.86).
Rejected: UN membership in no way constitutes a limitation on sovereignty (p.86).
Rejected: the book says neither fact limits sovereignty, internal or external (p.86).

questions.q: The Class 7 chapter says people often use 'the state' and 'the government' as if they meant the same thing. The reason it gives for this habit is that
questions.a: the government acts on behalf of the state and is the face of the state that people see in action every day
o: the government acts on behalf of the state and is the face of the state that people see in action every day
the two are the same body, and the difference between them is only one of the words used in law
sovereignty is exercised by the government alone, so that the state has no existence apart from it
the Constitution defines the two words in an identical manner for every purpose of the document
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.146: the words are mixed up because the government runs the daily work of the state and people usually interact with the government, not the whole state.
w: Rejected: the chapter says the words are different in meaning (p.146).
Rejected: the state remains while governments change, so it has a separate existence (p.146).
Rejected: the chapter gives no such identical definition; it distinguishes the two (p.145-146).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the parts of a state, as explained in the Class 7 chapter:

1. People who merely visit a place and then move on, like tourists, are counted as the permanent population of that place.
2. A permanent population develops its own culture and society that identify with the geographically defined territory.
3. The boundaries of a state must follow natural features such as rivers or mountain ranges, and cannot be lines agreed upon by neighbours.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: tourists have no identification with the place; only those who identify with it and usually live there form the permanent population (p.145). Statement 2 is correct: p.145. Statement 3 is incorrect: the chapter says the boundaries are not necessarily geographical features but lines agreed upon by the neighbouring states (p.145). (Class 7 Social Science chapter)
w: '1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect: p.145
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.145
'3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.145

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the government:

1. The government is a group of people or a system that runs the country, and it includes leaders, ministers and officials.
2. The functions of the government include making laws, enforcing laws and resolving disputes.
3. In a democracy like India the government is expected to work for everyone's wellbeing and to protect people's rights and freedoms.
4. The chapter compares the state to the principal and teachers of a school, and the government to the school itself.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.146. Statement 2 is correct: p.146. Statement 3 is correct: p.148. Statement 4 is incorrect: the chapter compares the government to the principal and teachers, who may come and go, and the state to the school, which remains (p.146). (Class 7 Social Science chapter)
w: '1, 2 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.146
'2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.146
'1 and 3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.146

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the word 'sovereign' in the Preamble, according to Laxmikanth:

1. India's membership of the United Nations constitutes a limitation on her sovereignty in external affairs.
2. It implies that India is neither a dependency nor a dominion of any other nation and is free to conduct its own internal and external affairs.
3. Being a sovereign state, India acquired Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Goa, Daman and Diu, Puducherry and Sikkim after the commencement of the Constitution.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the book says membership of the United Nations is in no way a limitation on India's sovereignty (p.86). Statement 2 is correct: p.86. Statement 3 is correct: p.94. (Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble; Ch.6 Union and Its Territory)
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.86
'3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.86
'2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.94

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the meaning of 'State' in Article 12 of the Constitution, as explained by Laxmikanth:

1. It covers the executive and legislative organs of both the Union and the state governments.
2. Article 12 defines the term 'State' for the whole Constitution and not merely for Part III on Fundamental Rights.
3. It covers local authorities such as municipalities and panchayats, and authorities such as LIC, ONGC and SAIL.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.131. Statement 2 is incorrect: Article 12 defines the term for the purposes of Part III on Fundamental Rights (p.131). Statement 3 is correct: p.131. (Laxmikanth Ch.8 Fundamental Rights)
w: '1, 2 and 3' includes statement 2, which is incorrect: p.131
'3 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.131
'1 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.131

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 1 of the Constitution, as explained by Laxmikanth:

1. India is described as a 'Union of States' partly because the states have no right to secede from the federation.
2. The expression 'Union of India' covers only the states, while the 'Territory of India' also covers the union territories and territories that may be acquired.
3. The special provisions of Part XXI for states such as Maharashtra, Nagaland and Sikkim override the general provisions relating to the states as a class.
4. The union territories are directly administered by the governments of the states in which they are situated.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Ambedkar's two reasons: the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among states, and the states cannot secede (p.93). Statement 2 is correct: p.93. Statement 3 is correct: p.93. Statement 4 is incorrect: the union territories and acquired territories are directly administered by the Central Government (p.93). (Laxmikanth Ch.6 Union and Its Territory)
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.93
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.93
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 4, which is incorrect: p.93

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the union territories, according to Laxmikanth:

1. Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa, which are states today, were formerly union territories.
2. The union territories were constituted in 1956 by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act and the States Reorganisation Act.
3. Puducherry was acquired from the Portuguese, like Goa, Daman and Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
4. Till 1973 Lakshadweep was known as the Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.587. Statement 2 is correct: p.587. Statement 3 is incorrect: Puducherry was acquired from the French; Goa, Daman and Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli came from the Portuguese (p.587). Statement 4 is correct: p.587. (Laxmikanth Ch.41 Union Territories)
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.587
'1 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.587
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.587

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the state, as discussed in the Class 7 chapter:

1. The chapter quotes Kautilya's view that without a government society becomes chaotic, with the more powerful big fish eating the smaller fish.
2. The chapter says that the police and taxation are examples of powers which the state does not claim to exercise legitimately.
3. The chapter cites Kautilya as saying that the king, as the primary authority of the state, stands above Raja Dharma.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.151. Statement 2 is incorrect: the chapter says the state claims the legitimate use of power, for example through control by the police and taxation (p.151). Statement 3 is incorrect: Kautilya said the king has to follow Raja Dharma and have a good governance system (p.151). (Class 7 Social Science chapter)
w: '2 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.151
'1 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.151
'3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.151

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the powers of Parliament over the states, as explained by Laxmikanth:

1. Article 2 enables Parliament to admit into the Union, or to establish, new states that are not part of the Union at the time.
2. A bill under Article 3 needs the support of a special majority of Parliament, as in the case of a constitutional amendment.
3. Article 3 deals with the internal readjustment of the territories of the existing states and covers an alteration in the name of a state.
4. Parliament is not bound by the views of the state legislature, which is why India is called an indestructible union of destructible states.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.94. Statement 2 is incorrect: laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments under Article 368 and can be passed by a simple majority in the ordinary legislative process (p.95). Statement 3 is correct: p.94. Statement 4 is correct: p.94. (Laxmikanth Ch.6 Union and Its Territory)
w: '1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: p.95
'2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.95
'1 and 4 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.94

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the organs of government, as discussed in the Class 7 chapter:

1. The chapter assigns the carrying out of laws to the judiciary and the task of ensuring that laws are followed to the executive.
2. In daily life citizens mainly interact with the departments that form part of the executive.
3. The chapter says that a country whose legislature, executive and judiciary overlap cannot be a democracy.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the executive carries out laws and makes policies, while the judiciary ensures that laws are followed (p.144). Statement 2 is correct: p.148. Statement 3 is incorrect: the chapter says only that in some countries the three are separate and in others they may overlap (p.148); the United Kingdom and India both have parliamentary systems in which the executive sits within the legislature, and both are democracies (Laxmikanth Ch.13, p.208-209). (Class 7 Social Science chapter; Laxmikanth Ch.13)
w: '1 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.144
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.144
'1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect: p.144

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the territory of India:

1. According to Laxmikanth, India at present has twenty-eight states, eight union territories and no acquired territories.
2. The administration of the scheduled areas and tribal areas within the states is dealt with in the Seventh and Eighth Schedules.
3. The Constituent Assembly unanimously agreed on the traditional name 'Bharat' for the country.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.587. Statement 2 is incorrect: the Fifth and Sixth Schedules contain the separate provisions for scheduled areas and tribal areas (p.93). Statement 3 is incorrect: there was no unanimity, so a mix of 'India, that is, Bharat' was adopted (p.93). (Laxmikanth Ch.41 p.587; Ch.6 p.93) So the count of correct statements is 1.
w: Miscount: 1 of the 3 statements is correct, so "none" is wrong.
Miscount: 1 of the 3 statements is correct, so "only two" is wrong.
Miscount: 1 of the 3 statements is correct, so "all three" is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the creation of union territories:

1. Delhi and Chandigarh were made union territories because of their cultural distinctiveness.
2. Strategic importance was a reason for creating the union territories of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.
3. Puducherry was made a union territory on grounds of strategic importance, like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.
4. Chandigarh became a union territory in 1966.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Delhi and Chandigarh were created on political and administrative considerations (p.587). Statement 2 is correct: p.587. Statement 3 is incorrect: Puducherry, like Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, was created for its cultural distinctiveness (p.587). Statement 4 is correct: p.587. (Laxmikanth Ch.41 Union Territories) So the count of correct statements is 2.
w: Miscount: 2 of the 4 statements are correct, so "only one" is wrong.
Miscount: 2 of the 4 statements are correct, so "only three" is wrong.
Miscount: 2 of the 4 statements are correct, so "none" is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about changes of territory, according to Laxmikanth:

1. By Article 4, laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not treated as amendments under Article 368 and can be passed by a simple majority.
2. In the 1960 Berubari reference the Supreme Court held that Article 3 does not empower Parliament to cede Indian territory to a foreign country.
3. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled that settling a boundary dispute with another country needs no constitutional amendment.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.95. Statement 2 is correct: p.95. Statement 3 is correct: p.95. (Laxmikanth Ch.6 Union and Its Territory) So the count of correct statements is 3.
w: Miscount: 3 of the 3 statements are correct, so "only two" is wrong.
Miscount: 3 of the 3 statements are correct, so "only one" is wrong.
Miscount: 3 of the 3 statements are correct, so "none" is wrong.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: Under the 100th Constitutional Amendment Act (2015) India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, while Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India.
Statement-II: The Radcliffe Award of 1947 settled every dispute on the India-East Pakistan boundary, so no later award or agreement was needed.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
o: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.6, p.95: the deal with Bangladesh involved 111 enclaves transferred by India and 51 by Bangladesh, so Statement-I is correct. Disputes arose out of some provisions of the Radcliffe Award and were sought to be resolved through the Bagge Award of 1950 and the Nehru-Noon Agreement of 1958, so Statement-II is incorrect.
w: Rejected: Statement-II is incorrect, so there is nothing for it to explain (p.95).
Rejected: Statement-II is incorrect, so the pair cannot both be correct (p.95).
Rejected: Statement-I is correct; the enclave numbers are on p.95.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The Constitution does not guarantee the territorial integrity or continued existence of any state of the Indian Union.
Statement-II: In the USA the continued existence of a state is guaranteed by the Constitution, and the federal government cannot alter its borders without its consent.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.6, p.94-95: Parliament can form new states or alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing states without their consent, so India is an indestructible union of destructible states; in the USA the continued existence of a state is guaranteed, hence an indestructible union of indestructible states. Both statements are correct, but Statement-II is a contrast and does not explain why Indian states are not guaranteed.
w: Rejected: the American position is a contrast; it does not cause the Indian position (p.94-95).
Rejected: Statement-II is correct (p.94-95).
Rejected: Statement-I is correct (p.94).

questions.q:
Match the term in List-I with its meaning in List-II, as given in the Class 7 chapter and by Laxmikanth.

List-I
A. Union of India
B. Territory of India
C. Sovereignty
D. State (for Part III)

List-II
1. Includes the Union and state governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities
2. Includes only the states
3. The full power to make laws and take decisions without any outside control
4. Includes the states, the union territories and territories that may be acquired
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.6, p.93: the Union of India includes only the states, while the Territory of India also covers the union territories and territories that may be acquired. Class 7 chapter, p.144: sovereignty is the full power to make laws and take decisions without outside control. Laxmikanth Ch.8, p.131: Article 12 defines 'State' for Part III.
w: A and B are interchanged: the Union of India is the narrower term, the Territory of India the wider (p.93).
C and D are interchanged: sovereignty is the power of the state, while Article 12 lists the bodies called State (p.131, 144).
A and C are interchanged: the Union of India is not sovereignty, and sovereignty is not a list of territories (p.93, 144).

concepts.name: The police, government departments and the people
concepts.description: The role of the police, how citizens relate to the government and the executive departments we meet in daily life.
concepts.idea: The police are part of state governments and protect people while respecting their rights.
concepts.rule: The police maintain law and order within each state and are part of the state government working with local communities. They are agents of the state who can legally use force to ensure safety free from crime and violence, work with courts and prisons, and promote safety through awareness programmes on road safety, drug abuse and women's safety, but must respect constitutional rights. People elect leaders to represent them, the police enforce laws and present cases to the judiciary, and the Constitution, laws and courts protect rights. Government departments, whose names we see on boards, implement policies made by the legislature; the judiciary ensures laws are followed. In daily life we mainly meet the executive.
concepts.example: Road safety awareness is part of police work.

questions.q: The Class 7 chapter says that the police are part of the state government. This agrees with the Seventh Schedule, in which 'public order' and 'police' appear in
questions.a: the State List, on which the state legislature normally has exclusive power to make laws
o: the State List, on which the state legislature normally has exclusive power to make laws
the Union List, on which Parliament alone is empowered to make laws for the whole country
the Concurrent List, on which both legislatures may legislate and the central law prevails in a conflict
the residuary list, the subjects of which belong to Parliament because the Constitution names none of them
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.147: the police maintain law and order within each state and are part of the state government. Laxmikanth Ch.15, p.222: the State List includes public order, police, prisons and public health.
w: Rejected: the Union List holds defence, banking, foreign affairs and the like, not police (p.222).
Rejected: criminal law and procedure are in the Concurrent List, but police and public order are in the State List (p.222).
Rejected: residuary matters are those in no list; police is expressly in the State List (p.222-223).

questions.q: A man is arrested by the police on a charge under an ordinary criminal law. Among the safeguards of the first part of Article 22, as explained by Laxmikanth, the police must
questions.a: produce him before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time taken on the journey
o: produce him before a magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time taken on the journey
produce him before a magistrate within 24 hours, counting the time taken on the journey
produce him before the nearest High Court judge within 48 hours of the arrest
produce him before an advisory board of High Court judges if the custody is to exceed three months
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.8, p.152: a person arrested under an ordinary law has the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner, and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours excluding the journey time, and to be released after 24 hours unless the magistrate authorises further detention.
w: Rejected: the journey time is excluded from the 24 hours, not counted in it (p.152).
Rejected: the safeguard is production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, not before a High Court judge within 48 hours (p.152).
Rejected: the advisory board is a safeguard of the second part of Article 22, for preventive detention, not for ordinary arrest (p.152).

questions.q: A state police force is unable to investigate a large case of corruption and the Central Bureau of Investigation wishes to take it up. As explained by Laxmikanth, the CBI can exercise its powers in that state, outside railway areas, only with
questions.a: the consent of the Government of that state
o: the consent of the Government of that state
a notification issued by the Supreme Court on the request of the Central Government
the prior approval of the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India
the written order of the Governor of that state acting in his discretion
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.65, p.716: the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 does not enable the CBI to exercise its powers and jurisdiction in any area of a state (not being a railway area) without the consent of the state government concerned.
w: Rejected: the Supreme Court has no such role under the Act (p.716).
Rejected: the Act requires the state government's consent, not the President's approval (p.716).
Rejected: it is the state government's consent that is needed, not a discretionary order of the Governor (p.716).

questions.q: Which one of the following agencies was constituted after the 2008 Mumbai terror attack, mainly for the investigation of terrorist attacks and terror funding, and works under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs?
questions.a: The National Investigation Agency, set up under the NIA Act, 2008
o: The National Investigation Agency, set up under the NIA Act, 2008
The Central Bureau of Investigation, set up under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946
The Central Vigilance Commission, given statutory status by the CVC Act, 2003
The Special Police Establishment, set up in 1941 for the War and Supply Department
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.67, p.729: the NIA was constituted in 2009 under the NIA Act, 2008 after the 26/11 attacks and works under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Ch.65, p.716: the CBI investigates corruption, economic offences and serious organised crime other than terrorism.
w: Rejected: the CBI deals with corruption and other serious crime other than terrorism, and long predates 2008 (p.716).
Rejected: the CVC is the main agency for preventing corruption in the Central Government (p.711).
Rejected: the Special Police Establishment was a wartime body to investigate bribery (p.716).

questions.q: Policing is a state subject, yet Article 355 casts two duties on the Union. Besides the duty to protect every state against external aggression and internal disturbance, the second duty under that Article, according to Laxmikanth, is to
questions.a: ensure that the government of every state is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution
o: ensure that the government of every state is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution
ensure that no state legislature is dissolved before the end of its term without the approval of Parliament
ensure that the police force of every state is placed under the superintendence of the Central Home Ministry
provide every state with a Central grant to meet the cost of maintaining its police force
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.15, p.229: Article 355 imposes two duties on the Centre, (a) to protect every state against external aggression and internal disturbance, and (b) to ensure that the government of every state is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
w: Rejected: Article 355 contains no condition on the dissolution of a state legislature; that is not a duty it imposes (p.229).
Rejected: Article 355 does not place state police under the Centre; police remains a State List subject (p.222, 229).
Rejected: the second duty concerns constitutional government in every state, not funding for the police (p.229).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the police, as described in the Class 7 chapter:

1. The police work separately from the courts and the prisons and are not a part of the criminal justice system.
2. The police maintain law and order within each state and work directly with local communities in towns, cities and villages.

concepts.name: Democracy, republic and protecting everyone's rights
concepts.description: The difference between democracy and republic, India as a democratic republic, protection of minorities and the tribal lands example.
concepts.idea: In a democratic republic the people elect the government and the head of state is elected within limits set by a constitution.
concepts.rule: Democracy means rule by the people (demos = people, kratos = rule): people choose their government through free and fair elections. A republic is a form of government where the head of state is elected, directly or indirectly, and not a hereditary monarch, and where the ruler's power is limited by a constitution or laws. A country can be both, like India or the USA. The UK, Canada and Sweden are democracies but not republics as they have monarchs. India's president is elected by a group of elected representatives. The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights so the majority cannot violate any citizen's rights, preventing 'dominance of the majority'. Mining was not allowed in the sacred hills of the Dongria Kondh. George Washington refused to become king in 1782.
concepts.example: The RWA changed its rule to exempt food and medicines, protecting a minority.

Rejected: a hereditary head of state means it is not a republic, whatever limits apply (p.149).

concepts.name: The legislature and the political and permanent executive
concepts.description: The legislature, the political executive, the permanent executive or bureaucracy and civil services.
concepts.idea: Elected leaders make big decisions while permanent civil servants run the government day to day.
concepts.rule: The legislature makes laws that apply to everyone; states have their own legislatures making laws for the state. The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions and has two parts. The political executive are elected leaders: the prime minister, chief ministers and ministers, and the president and governors, whom the chapter lists with mostly formal roles (Laxmikanth p.452 notes that the Governor is appointed by the President and is not elected). They serve a fixed time, usually five years. The permanent executive are officers selected through exams such as those by the UPSC, called bureaucrats or civil servants, who are not changed after elections and give expert advice, implement policies and manage services. Well-known services include IFS, IAS, IPS, IRS and IFoS. C.B. Muthamma became the first woman to join the Indian Foreign Service in 1949 and won a Supreme Court case against gender bias.
concepts.example: Grassroots bureaucrats include government school teachers, anganwadi workers and health workers.

concepts.description: Protector, provider and regulator roles, and ways citizens can act: grievance redressal, RTI, media, NGOs, letters and voting.
concepts.idea: Citizens can make government work for them through grievance offices, RTI, media, civil society, letters and voting.
concepts.rule: The government is protector (law and defence), provider (public welfare and infrastructure) and regulator (economic activity and social justice). Yet problems like corruption and poor services remain. Citizens can use grievance redressal offices and the Public Grievances Portal, ask for information under the Right to Information Act which brings transparency and accountability, use the media, engage through civil society organisations or NGOs, write to representatives and vote. In Bagepalli near Bengaluru an RTI on road spending helped citizens get poorly done roadwork fixed. In 1970 the Kerala Government planned a hydroelectric project in Silent Valley; NGOs, scientists and villagers opposed it, the Centre cancelled it in 1983 and it became a National Park in 1985.
concepts.example: The Silent Valley Movement saved rainforest from a dam.

questions.q: The Government builds roads, bridges, railways and airports and hires teachers to provide free schooling for children. Among the three roles of the Government of India described in the Class 7 chapter, this is the role of
questions.a: a provider, concerned with public welfare and infrastructure
o: a provider, concerned with public welfare and infrastructure
a protector, concerned with law and defence
a regulator, concerned with economic activity and social justice
a protector and regulator together, since both ensure public safety
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.156: the Government plays the triple role of protector (law and defence), provider (public welfare and infrastructure) and regulator (economic activity and social justice); providing free education by building schools and hiring teachers and constructing infrastructure are examples of provider.
w: Rejected: law and defence, as with the police forces, is the protector role (p.156).
Rejected: regulating economic activity and social justice is a different role from building infrastructure (p.156).
Rejected: the chapter lists three separate roles and places infrastructure and schooling under provider (p.156).

questions.q: A citizen wants to complain about a delay in obtaining information under the Right to Information Act from an office of the Central Government. The Central Information Commission, which looks into such complaints, is according to Laxmikanth
questions.a: a statutory body established in 2005 under the Right to Information Act, and not a constitutional body
o: a statutory body established in 2005 under the Right to Information Act, and not a constitutional body
a constitutional body provided for by an Article in Part XIV of the Constitution, on the pattern of the UPSC and the State Public Service Commissions
a statutory body created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee to prevent corruption
an executive body created in 2005 by a Cabinet resolution without any statutory backing
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.62, p.704: the Central Information Commission was established by the Central Government in 2005 under the provisions of the Right to Information Act (2005) and is not a constitutional body; it looks into complaints and decides appeals.
w: Rejected: the Commission is not a constitutional body (p.704).
Rejected: the 1964 body on the Santhanam Committee's recommendation is the Central Vigilance Commission (p.711).
Rejected: the Commission was constituted under the provisions of the Act, so it has statutory backing (p.704).

questions.q: According to the Class 7 chapter, in 1970 the Kerala Government planned a large hydroelectric project in the Silent Valley, which was opposed by non-government organisations, scientists and villagers. The sequel described in the Class 7 chapter is that
questions.a: the Central Government cancelled the project in 1983, and two years later the Silent Valley was declared a National Park
o: the Central Government cancelled the project in 1983, and two years later the Silent Valley was declared a National Park
the Kerala High Court quashed the project in 1980 on a petition by the villagers, and in 1983 the Silent Valley was declared a National Park
the Kerala Government itself withdrew the project in 1975, and in 1980 the Silent Valley was declared a National Park
the Central Government approved a smaller project in 1983, and in 1990 the Silent Valley was declared a National Park
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.159: many NGOs mobilised public opinion against the dam, soon joined by scientists, environmentalists, writers, teachers and villagers; in 1983 the Central Government intervened and cancelled the project, and two years later the Silent Valley was declared a National Park.
w: Rejected: the chapter credits the Central Government's intervention in 1983, not a court (p.159).
Rejected: it was the Central Government that cancelled the project, in 1983 (p.159).
Rejected: the project was cancelled, not scaled down, and the National Park came two years after 1983 (p.159).

questions.q: According to Laxmikanth, the institutions of Lokpal and Lokayukta for the redressal of citizens' grievances, on the pattern of the Ombudsman of the Scandinavian countries, were first recommended by
o: the Hanumantha Rao Committee on District Planning (1984)
the G.V.K. Rao Committee on rural development administration (1985)
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.66, p.723: the First Administrative Reforms Commission of India (1966-70) recommended the setting up of two special authorities, Lokpal and Lokayukta, on the pattern of the Ombudsman in Scandinavian countries.
w: Rejected: the book credits the First Administrative Reforms Commission of 1966-70, not a later commission (p.723).
Rejected: that committee of 1984 dealt with district planning, not grievance institutions (p.552).
Rejected: that committee of 1985 reviewed administrative arrangements for rural development (p.551).

questions.q: According to Laxmikanth, which one of the following was the first Commonwealth country in the world to adopt the Ombudsman system, in the form of a Parliamentary Commissioner for Investigation?
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.66, p.722: the Ombudsman was first created in Sweden in 1809 and spread to Finland (1919), Denmark (1955) and Norway (1962); New Zealand is the first Commonwealth country to have adopted it, as a Parliamentary Commissioner for Investigation in 1962, and the United Kingdom followed in 1967.
w: Rejected: the United Kingdom adopted an Ombudsman-like Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration in 1967, after New Zealand (p.722).
Rejected: Sweden created the institution in 1809, but it is not a Commonwealth country (p.721-722).
Rejected: Denmark adopted it in 1955 among the Scandinavian countries, but it is not a Commonwealth country (p.722).

Consider the following statements:

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

concepts.name: The judiciary: guardian of the Constitution
concepts.description: What the judiciary does, judicial review, the rule of law and why independence matters.
concepts.idea: The independent judiciary protects rights, interprets laws and ensures everyone follows the law.
concepts.rule: The judiciary makes sure everyone follows the law. It settles disputes, protects people's rights and checks whether laws made by government are fair and just. It is independent, not controlled by government or politicians, so justice is fair and equal. Its functions are protecting and defending laws, interpreting laws when wording is complex or people disagree, protecting citizens' rights and liberty (we can go to court if fundamental rights are violated) and safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review, acting as a referee when government or others break the law. It protects the rule of law: everyone, even the government, must follow the law. Without a strong and fair judiciary, democracy cannot survive.
concepts.example: Judicial review lets courts check whether laws follow the Constitution.

questions.q: A law passed by a legislature is challenged in court as going against the Constitution. Of the functions of the judiciary listed in the Class 7 chapter, the one that the chapter describes as acting like a referee when the government or others break the law is
questions.a: safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review
o: safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review
protecting and defending the laws by making sure they are followed properly
interpreting the laws when their wording is complex or people disagree on their meaning
protecting the rights and liberty of citizens through the courts when fundamental rights are violated
questions.e: Class 7 Social Science chapter, p.160: the fourth function of the judiciary is to safeguard the Constitution through judicial review, acting as a referee when the government or others break the law. The other three are defending laws, interpreting them and protecting the rights and liberty of citizens.
w: Rejected: this function is about making sure laws are followed; the referee role is attached to judicial review (p.160).
Rejected: interpretation explains what a law means; it does not test a law against the Constitution (p.160).
Rejected: this function is the protection of rights; the referee role goes with judicial review (p.160).

questions.q: Judicial review in India is best described, according to Laxmikanth, as
questions.a: the power of the courts to test the laws and executive orders of the Centre and the states against the Constitution and to declare violating ones void
o: the power of the courts to test the laws and executive orders of the Centre and the states against the Constitution and to declare violating ones void
the power of the President to refer a question of law or fact to the Supreme Court for its opinion under Article 143, which the Court must answer
the power of Parliament to set aside a judgment of a court by passing an ordinary law that removes the basis of the judgment
the power of the Supreme Court to hear appeals from the high courts in constitutional cases
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.27, p.431: judicial review is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders of both Central and state governments and to declare them null and void if they violate the Constitution.
w: Rejected: that is the advisory jurisdiction of Article 143, not judicial review (p.433).
Rejected: judicial review is exercised by the courts, not by Parliament over courts (p.431).
Rejected: that is the appellate jurisdiction of the Court under Article 132 (p.433).

questions.q: A judge of the Supreme Court holds office until the age of 65 years. Apart from resignation, the Constitution permits his removal only by
questions.a: an order of the President after an address by both Houses, by special majority, in the same session, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
o: an order of the President after an address by both Houses, by special majority, in the same session, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
an order of the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers, since the judge is appointed by the President and holds office at his pleasure
a recommendation of the collegium of the four seniormost judges, accepted by the Chief Justice of India and the President on the advice of ministers
an order of the President after an address by the Lok Sabha alone, supported by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.26, p.416: the President can issue the removal order only after an address by Parliament has been presented to him in the same session, supported by a special majority of each House, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity; p.418: judges do not hold office during the pleasure of the President.
w: Rejected: judges do not hold office during the pleasure of the President or the ministers (p.418).
Rejected: the collegium is concerned with appointment, not removal (p.414-415).
Rejected: the address must be supported by a special majority of each House of Parliament, not by the Lok Sabha alone (p.416).

questions.q: In 2015 the Supreme Court declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act of 2014 unconstitutional. According to Laxmikanth, the Court's opinion was that the new system would
questions.a: affect the independence of the judiciary, and the collegium system consequently became operative again
o: affect the independence of the judiciary, and the collegium system consequently became operative again
violate the federal structure, since the states had no place on the Commission
reduce the retirement age of judges, and the earlier age limit consequently became operative again
transfer the power of appointment to the Prime Minister, and the earlier convention consequently became operative again
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.26, p.415: in the Fourth Judges case (2015) the Court opined that the NJAC would affect the independence of the judiciary; the collegium system became operative again. Ch.27, p.431 records the same verdict.
w: Rejected: the stated ground was the independence of the judiciary, not federalism (p.415).
Rejected: the NJAC dealt with appointment, not with the retirement age (p.415).
Rejected: the stated ground was the effect on judicial independence (p.415).

questions.q: A citizen whose fundamental right is violated may move the Supreme Court directly under Article 32 or a high court under Article 226. According to Laxmikanth, the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is
questions.a: not exclusive, since the high courts are also empowered to issue writs for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights
o: not exclusive, since the high courts are also empowered to issue writs for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights
exclusive, since only the Supreme Court may issue the writs of habeas corpus and certiorari
wider than that of a high court, since the Supreme Court may issue writs for any purpose and not only for Fundamental Rights
available only after the aggrieved citizen has failed to obtain relief in a high court by way of appeal
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.26, p.420: the Supreme Court can issue writs, including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights; its original writ jurisdiction is concurrent with the high courts, and a high court can issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for other purposes too.
w: Rejected: the high courts too can issue the writs (p.420).
Rejected: the Supreme Court issues writs only for Fundamental Rights, while a high court can do so for other purposes as well (p.420).
Rejected: the aggrieved party has the option of moving either court directly (p.420).

Consider the following statements about what the judiciary does, according to the Class 7 chapter:

1. It protects and defends the laws by making sure that they are followed properly.
2. It interprets the laws, explaining what a law means when the wording is complex or people disagree on its meaning.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the rule of law, according to the Class 7 chapter and Laxmikanth:

1. The Class 7 chapter says the judiciary protects the rule of law, the idea that everyone must follow the law, even the government.
2. According to Laxmikanth, all three elements of Dicey's rule of law apply to the Indian system.
3. According to Laxmikanth, the first two elements of Dicey's rule of law, absence of arbitrary power and equality before the law, apply to the Indian system.

concepts.name: Tiers of government and decentralisation
concepts.description: The three tiers, why India needs decentralisation, panchayats and municipalities, Gandhi's gram swaraj and the education example.
concepts.idea: Power is shared among union, state and local governments so that local problems are solved locally.
concepts.rule: India has three tiers of government: union (central), state and local. India has 28 states and 8 union territories and over 1.4 billion people, so a single government cannot meet all needs. The Constitution originally had only two levels; local governments were under the State List. In the early 1990s amendments created the panchayati raj system and municipalities as the third tier, strengthening democracy at the grassroots. Decentralisation means power is spread out and local problems are solved locally, with bigger issues by higher governments. Benefits are stronger local governments, better local knowledge, more democracy, local discussion and more accountability. The union looks after defence, foreign affairs and currency; states handle police, land, health and agriculture; local governments handle water, drainage and streetlamps. Gandhi advocated gram swaraj. In school education, Parliament and state legislatures make laws like the Right to Education Act, ministers and officers implement them and courts and bodies like NCPCR protect children's rights.
concepts.example: A broken streetlamp is fixed by the local municipal body, not the Central Government.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: Elections to panchayats and municipalities no longer depend on the will of the state government.
Statement-II: The 73rd and 74th Amendments brought the local bodies under the justiciable part of the Constitution and made the state governments constitutionally obliged to adopt the new systems.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.39, p.554-555 and Ch.40, p.571: the two Acts give panchayats and municipalities constitutional status, bring them under the justiciable part of the Constitution and oblige the states to adopt the new systems, so the formation of the bodies and regular elections no longer depend on the state government's will. Statement-II explains Statement-I.
w: Rejected: the constitutional obligation on the states is why elections no longer depend on their will (p.555).
Rejected: Statement-II is correct (p.554, 571).
Rejected: Statement-I is correct (p.555).
